reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AABB Technical Manual
clinicalPearls: Occurs when haemoglobin iron is oxidised from the ferrous to the ferric state, producing methaemoglobin that cannot bind oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve so remaining oxygen is released poorly
Classic clue is cyanosis, often with chocolate-brown blood, that does not improve with supplemental oxygen
A characteristic saturation gap exists, with pulse oximetry reading falsely and tending toward the mid-80s while arterial blood gas calculates a normal partial pressure of oxygen
Co-oximetry, not standard oximetry or blood gas calculation, is required to measure the methaemoglobin fraction directly
Acquired causes predominate and include oxidant drugs and chemicals such as topical and local anaesthetics, dapsone, nitrites and nitrates, and aniline compounds
Congenital forms arise from cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency or from haemoglobin M variants and are usually better tolerated because of chronic adaptation

First-line treatment of significant symptomatic acquired disease is methylene blue, which is ineffective and potentially harmful in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, where exchange transfusion or ascorbic acid may be considered
reference.pathophysiology: Haemoglobin normally keeps its iron in the reduced ferrous state, which binds oxygen; a small fraction is continually oxidised to the ferric methaemoglobin form and reduced again, mainly by the cytochrome b5 reductase (NADH-dependent) system. Methaemoglobinaemia develops when oxidative stress from drugs or chemicals overwhelms this reducing capacity, or when the reductase enzyme or the globin chain is congenitally abnormal. Ferric haem cannot carry oxygen, and its presence increases the oxygen affinity of the remaining ferrous haem, impairing oxygen delivery to tissues. The NADPH-dependent methaemoglobin reductase pathway becomes relevant therapeutically because methylene blue acts through it, which is why it fails when glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is deficient.
additionalDifferentials: Shock or peripheral cyanosis from low cardiac output
additionalInvestigations: Co-oximetry to quantify the methaemoglobin fraction
Arterial blood gas alongside pulse oximetry to demonstrate the saturation gap
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase assay before or alongside methylene blue use
Review of drug, chemical, and occupational exposures
Enzyme assay or haemoglobin analysis when a congenital form is suspected
redFlags: Symptomatic hypoxia with high methaemoglobin levels causing altered consciousness, seizures, arrhythmia, or cardiovascular collapse, which is an emergency
Suspected methaemoglobinaemia in a patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, where methylene blue is hazardous
Rapidly rising levels after a large oxidant exposure
reference.prognosis: Acquired disease usually resolves well once the offending agent is removed and, where needed, methylene blue is given; congenital reductase deficiency is generally compatible with normal life, whereas very high acute levels can be fatal without prompt treatment.
pitfalls: Trusting pulse oximetry or a calculated blood gas saturation instead of measuring methaemoglobin by co-oximetry
Persisting with oxygen alone when cyanosis fails to respond
Giving methylene blue in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, risking haemolysis and worsening
Failing to identify and stop the causative oxidant exposure
management: For acquired disease, remove the offending oxidant agent and give methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) for symptomatic elevation
Check glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status before methylthioninium chloride and use ascorbic acid, exchange transfusion, or hyperbaric oxygen if deficient
Treat congenital cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency, when troublesome, with chronic oral methylthioninium chloride or ascorbic acid, though many need no treatment
Provide supplemental oxygen and monitor the methaemoglobin fraction with co-oximetry
Educate susceptible and congenital patients to avoid oxidant drugs and chemicals
Reserve exchange transfusion and critical care for severe or refractory acute elevations
Offer genetic counselling for congenital reductase deficiency and haemoglobin M variants, the latter usually requiring no therapy
